newsitem.title: FRANCE: Green Euro-MPs attack new rules on gene-food.
newsitem.headline: Green Euro-MPs attack new rules on gene-food.

text.p: Green Euro-MPs on Wednesday slammed a draft regulation on novel foods, which include goods containing genetically-modified organisms, saying it did not offer proper consumer protection.
"We think it is a second class compromise, second class consumer protection, because it doesn't provide for comprehensive labelling," German Green Hiltrud Breyer told a news conference.

The parliament is due to vote on Thursday on regulation COM(93)631, which sets binding Europe-wide rules for the marketing of foodstuffs produced with new technology or being sold for the first time in Europe.
The environmental group Greenpeace has urged Euro-MPs to heed a new survey showing that a majority of voters oppose the development of genetically-modified food.
Genetic engineering allows beer to ferment faster, cheese to mature quicker, pigs to grow larger, tomatoes to age more slowly and cereals to resist pests.
Greenpeace said it feared that, after six years of negotiations with the European Commission and Council of Ministers, Euro-MPs were exhausted and likely to approve the new rules.
The novel foods regulation is subject to new co-decision procedures giving the parliament the right to veto legislation.

In a report presented to the parliament, German Socialist Dagmar Roth-Behrendt said the final compromise was inadequate but insisted that consumers, manufacturers and traders would all prefer imperfect binding European rules to a legal vacuum.
Breyer said the Greens were alarmed at loopholes and exceptions in the new rules. They wanted all foods containing genetically-manipulated organisms to be labelled clearly.

She said consumers would be warned only if a living genetically-altered element was present in the final product or if scientific analysis showed novel foods to be significantly different from conventional ones.

There would be no obligation, for example, to label milk from cows fed on genetically-modified grains or sweets made from genetically-modified suger beet. "Consumers are again left in the dark," Breyer said.

In many cases, scientific methods did not exist to demonstrate the difference between a novel and a traditional food, she said, adding that this would pose a particular worry for people with allergies.
Belgian Green Paul Lannoye said enzymes, flavourings and additives were all exempt from the regulation.
Breyer said that, even where labels were required, there would be no standard format and manufacturers could more or less put what they liked. "All this simply leads to consumer confusion," she said.
The Greens are also concerned at a compromise on a particularly controversial point which was thrashed out by parliament and Council of Ministers negotiating teams on November 28, 1996.
The parliament dropped its demand for bulk deliveries containing both conventional and genetically-modified types of soya, maize and other goods to be labelled.
In return, the council agreed that suppliers could use "negative labelling" stressing that their products did not contain genetically-altered substances.
Lannoye raised the spectre of mad cow disease and trans- Atlantic rows about pumping growth hormones into cattle as further reasons for extreme caution in tampering with nature.
"This is a new technology and we're just heading into the fog. We don't know much about this and the risks to health," he said.

The survey highlighted by Greenpeace, which came from Market & Opinion Research International (MORI), said 59 percent of the Danes, Dutch, French, British, Italians and Swedes questioned were opposed to genetically-engineered food.
Resistance was strongest in Sweden, where 76 percent were against, and lowest in Italy, where 44 percent were opposed.
A separate German survey by market research Institut GfK found that 74 percent of those covered wanted to stop gene-food.
